Hungarian is a Uralic language spoken primarily in Hungary and neighboring regions, linguistically isolated within Central Europe by being one of the few non-Indo-European languages in the region. It is the most widely spoken Uralic language, and its nearest relatives are Finnish and Estonian. Hungarian has about 10 million native speakers concentrated in Hungary, with additional diaspora communities scattered around the world. The language uses an agglutinative structure with 18 to 20 noun cases depending on classification and numerous postpositions rather than prepositions, creating lengthy, information-packed words that challenge learners from Indo-European backgrounds. Vowel harmony is a prominent feature, with vowels in suffix patterns agreeing with the vowels in the stem, distinguishing front vowels from back vowels. Word order is flexible, with SVO, SOV, and other patterns occurring naturally, and verbs conjugate for person, number, and definiteness, marking whether the object is definite or indefinite. The language has an extensive vocabulary of Finno-Ugric roots alongside significant borrowing from Slavic, Germanic, and Romance languages due to geographic contact. Hungarian has been spoken continuously in the Carpathian Basin since the Magyar migration in the ninth century, and the language has evolved remarkably little in its core structure across that millennium. Hungarian exemplifies productive agglutination with complex case systems and stands as a standard example in typological surveys of agglutinative and postpositional languages.
